item.title: Diseases in Russian Permafrost May Be Scarier Than Plague
item.description: After the Covid pandemic, we’re all a little jumpy when it comes to new disease outbreaks. So it’s understandable that the death of a lab technician working at a plague research institute in Siberia has put everyone on high alert. But while there’s still much we don’t know about that case, there is another health threat brewing in Russia that deserves more attention and alarm.
item.dc:creator: Lara Williams

item.title: Best Restaurant Lists Are One Reason Why Fine Dining Is Struggling
item.description: Bruno Verjus, the restaurant-critic-turned-chef, reignited an old debate in July when he announced he was shutting down Table, his two-Michelin-starred Paris restaurant. His provocation: “Fine dining is dead.” It was too exclusive. Too expensive. Too isolated from the realities of a world of pocketbook-conscious ordinary people. He wasn’t saying anything original.
item.dc:creator: Howard Chua-Eoan

item.title: US Bases Overseas Are Becoming Prime Targets
item.description: The Pentagon’s abrupt withdrawal of a dozen long-range B-1 bombers from a British airbase this week raises a host of troubling questions. Vice President J.D. Vance said the move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after US and British officials reportedly received warnings of a potential drone attack ordered by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
item.dc:creator: James Stavridis

item.title: EU’s €800 Billion of Covid Borrowing Was a Good Start
item.description: Six years ago, the European Union’s ambitious €800 billion post-Covid recovery program was hailed by some as the bloc’s “Hamiltonian moment.” As the money runs out, a humbler verdict makes more sense.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: It’d Be Super Intelligent to Stop Trying to Rebrand AI
item.description: Trump’s push to call AI “super intelligence” is a silly side quest.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: The Next AI Race Exposes the Limits of Language
item.description: More than 50 years after her death, Helen Keller still turns up in artificial intelligence debates. The communication breakthroughs of the American writer, who was deaf and blind, are often cited as evidence that language is the best path to creating machines that are as intelligent as humans.
item.dc:creator: Catherine Thorbecke

item.title: Europe Has Got Its Made-in-China Policy Wrong
item.description: If the definition of madness is doing the same thing again and again and expecting a different result, what are we to make of the latest broadsides in the trade war brewing between the European Union and China?
item.dc:creator: David Fickling

item.title: Pre-IPO Perpetual Futures Swap ETF
item.description: Corgi MANGOS, prime brokerage, longshot predictions and AGM buffet arbitrage.
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine

item.title: The World Isn’t Ready for a Japan With Interest
item.description: Two years ago, when Japan embarked on its path toward policy normalization, I asked whether the country was ready for a “world with interest.” It was a question many were asking as the Asian nation rediscovered inflation and non-zero interest rates after decades without either.
item.dc:creator: Gearoid Reidy

item.title: Starbucks Should Avoid a Grande-Sized Gamble on Chipotle
item.description: Starbucks Corp. has reportedly explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. in what would be the biggest restaurant deal of all time. It’s unclear whether Starbucks is still pursuing a tie-up, or if it has dropped the idea. It should do the latter and avoid creating a slop bowl with a side of cold brew.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Felsted

item.title: Chapek and Iger’s Feud Embarrasses Disney Amid Layoffs
item.description: Bob Chapek and Bob Iger may no longer run Walt Disney Co., but lately the two former CEOs have been doing the company a favor.
item.dc:creator: Beth Kowitt

item.title: Adam Hamilton Makes Kansas Worth More of Democrats’ Midterm Money
item.description: Yes, Democrats have a shot in Kansas.
item.dc:creator: Nia-Malika Henderson

item.title: AI Giants Are Facing a Severe Case of Indigestion on Chips and Data Centers
item.description: Amid heated discussion of the astonishing (and also rather worrying) capabilities of artificial intelligence, investors are realizing that the underlying computing and energy infrastructure relied upon by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC and their ilk is much harder to construct than a chatbot prompt.
item.dc:creator: Chris Bryant

item.title: US Healthcare Risks Undermining Economic Growth Without Reform
item.description: Consumer confidence is collapsing, hiring is weak and the housing market is largely frozen. All of which serves to underscore that the US economy is only holding up because of the boom in artificial intelligence and an aging population spending ever more on healthcare. Although the former seems to garner all the attention these days, the latter is becoming a rising source of vulnerability. item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: AI Doom: Prepare for Risk, Prioritize Safety, Don't Panic
item.description: “Nobody knows anything,” the screenwriter William Goldman famously said of the movie business. Much the same can be said today for artificial intelligence, a technology that’s moving fast, destination unknown. Unlike movies, though, the bots may one day rise up and exterminate humanity, according to some in the industry. It’s fair to say that people are worried.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Trump’s Public Relations Excuse Masks Deeper Political Failures
item.description: Complaining about subpar public relations is the last refuge of the political loser. It’s a bipartisan affliction that surfaces in every American election, including this year’s midterm campaign. President Donald Trump is patient zero this time.
item.dc:creator: David M. Drucker

item.title: A New Steel Plant in Iowa Shows the Lunacy of Trump's Tariff Policy
item.description: With great fanfare, President Donald Trump announced last week that “the largest steel plant ever built in the United States” would be coming to Lee County, Iowa, adding that Mesabi Metallics’ $15 billion investment in a pivotal midterm swing state proved his “powerful 50% tariffs” were working. He’s right: The announcement is a tangible result of American steel policy — but, contrary to what the president said, that’s not a good thing.
item.dc:creator: Scott Lincicome

item.title: It’s a Depressing Time to Care About Free Markets
item.description: Free-market-oriented economists probably live in a state of perpetual despair these days. Politicians and voters on both the left and right are turning on markets. Polls suggest widespread support for interventionist policies that economists long discarded for causing more harm than good.
item.dc:creator: Allison Schrager

item.title: Green Party: British Anti-Semitism Has Made a Distressing Return
item.description: This week should have been a triumph for the UK’s Green Party. Instead, it finds itself a pariah; riven internally, isolated politically and condemned globally, thanks to a toxic embrace of hardline anti-Zionism. Its stance has brought shame to one of the world’s oldest environmental parties, a once admirable movement dedicated to confronting the climate disaster long before it was fashionable.
item.dc:creator: Rosa Prince
